subject: Is it okay to analyze covariation ratios as a function of Procrustes distances?

messages.author: 9d868dc7ec0156e3
messages.subject: Is it okay to analyze covariation ratios as a function of Procrustes distances?
parts:
Hey everyone! 

I am analyzing modularity, integration, and disparity across turtles. I have linear measurements of limbs, shells, and heads, not landmark data. I am testing several modularity hypotheses using the phy.modularity function and I have pruned the phylogenetic tree i'm using and my data so that I can test these modularity hypothesis separately for all turtles and for each major turtle clade. Therefore, for any particular modularity hypothesis, I run the analysis for all turtles in my data set, then for each subsequent turtle clade. So for each hypothesis I have a covariation ratio (CR) coefficient and a P-value for all turtles, and each family. Then, I have used the morphol.disparity function in the data set with all the turtles to measure morphological disparity in the proposed modules across all turtle clades. 

I ask if it is acceptable to regress CR coefficients against Procustes variances to explore relationships between modularity and disparity? 

Attached is an example. On the x-axis are CR coefficients from one of the well supported supported modularity hypothesis in which all the measurements I took of the legs and shell are one module, and the measurements of the head is another module. This hypothesis is also depicted by colors in the turtle silhouette. On the Y-axis are Procustes variances (although since I have linear measurements aren't they euclidean variances?) of the whole turtle body. Therefore, the disparity values correspond to the overall disparity of each major turtle clade, meaning the n x variables matrix I input into the function contains limb, shell, and head measurements. There are six major turtle clades in this graph, emydids (sliders and box turtles), geoemydids (old world wood turtles), pleurodira (side-neck turtles), kinosternids (mud turtles, stink-pots, snappers), testudinids (tortoises), trionychids (soft-shell turtles). 

If I want to know if the strength of covariation between modules among turtle clades is related to morphology disparity of that clade is this okay to do? 

Thank you so much for any insight. 

Muchos saludos, 
            Taggert 

P.S. in X-axis it says high values= more integrated. I now realize that that isn't necessarily the case.

messages.author: 511e44c7d1e1bab0
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Is it okay to analyze covariation ratios as a function of Procrustes distances?
parts:
Taggert,

I see nothing fundamentally wrong with regressing CR vs. variance to test for the suggested relationship between modularity and disparity. Why you would predict a non-linear relationship, as your graph suggests, or a linear one for that respect is another issue, which you need to consider from first principles beforehand. A useful recent read on the whole subject is the article by Felice et al Evolution (doi: 10.1111/evo.13608)

As for using morphol.disparity on linear measurements, yes, this is fine, as in that case you will obtain the sum of diagonal elements of the (group) covariance matrix divided by (group) sample size. This is called the Procrustes variance because it was put forward as a measure of disparity in the context of GM, but it can be used with any kind of data.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

messages.author: 511e44c7d1e1bab0
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Is it okay to analyze covariation ratios as a function of Procrustes distances?
parts: For non-GM data I would not call them Procrustes variances, but they are fully equivalent. Essentially this comes from using the term "Procrustes distance" as an equivalent to the Euclidean distance of each observation from the group´s centroid calculated over superimposed coordinates projected to tangent space. See chapter 12, Disparity and Variation, in Zelditch et al. 2012 Geometric Morphometrics for Biologists for the formulae and correspondence between variance metrics.
